summary: After praying alone before dawn, Jesus leaves the crowds of Capernaum to preach in the synagogues of all Galilee, and His fame spreads far beyond it.
key_insight: The morning after Capernaum’s great night of healing, Simon brought what sounded like good news: “Everyone is looking for You.” Jesus answered by leaving. He measured His work not by the crowd at the door but by the purpose He was sent for.
story: Early the next morning, after the crowded evening at the door in Capernaum, Jesus rose a long while before daylight. He went out to a solitary place, and there He prayed. {Mk}

Simon and the others with Him went searching for Him. When they found Him, they said, “Everyone is looking for You.” {Mk} As the day came on, the crowd too sought Him out. They came to Him and tried to keep Him from leaving them. {Lk}

But Jesus said, “Let us go into the next towns, that I may preach there also, because for this purpose I have come forth.” {Mk} To the people who would have held on to Him He said, “I must preach the kingdom of God to the other cities also, because for this purpose I have been sent.” {Lk}

So He went through all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every kind of sickness and disease among the people. {Mt} He was casting out demons as well. {Mk}

His fame went throughout all Syria. People brought Him all who were sick with various diseases and torments: the demon-possessed, epileptics and paralytics. And He healed them. Great multitudes followed Him, from Galilee, and from Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan. {Mt}
differences: Only Mark says Jesus rose “a long while before daylight” and prayed. Luke says He went out “when it was day” and does not mention prayer.
In Mark, Simon and those with him search for Jesus and tell Him, “Everyone is looking for You.” In Luke, the crowd comes to Him and tries to keep Him from leaving.
Jesus says “for this purpose I have come forth” in Mark and “for this purpose I have been sent” in Luke.
Matthew has no morning scene. His summary alone tells of fame through “all Syria,” lists the kinds of sufferers brought, and names the regions the crowds came from.
Matthew places his summary right after the call of the four fishermen and before the Sermon on the Mount. Mark and Luke tie the tour to the morning after the Sabbath in Capernaum.

fit.question: Mark says Jesus went out a long while before daylight and that Simon and his companions found Him. Luke says He went out “when it was day” and that the crowd found Him. Which is it?

points.label: Two moments of one morning
points.text: Mark tells when Jesus left the house to pray, long before light. Luke’s “when it was day” marks the morning more broadly and moves straight to the moment the people found Him. McGarvey noted that each writer fixes on a different hour of the same morning.

points.label: First the friends, then the town
points.text: Simon and those with him tracked Jesus down first, and the townspeople were not far behind. Jesus’ answer served both: He would go on to other towns.

fit.note: Mark remembers the search as Simon’s group lived it; Luke tells how the town responded. Both fit one morning.
fit.short: Jesus left before light to pray; by daybreak His friends, and then the crowd, had found Him. Each writer tells a different part of the morning.

fit.question: In Luke 4:44 the NKJV says Jesus preached “in the synagogues of Galilee,” but many older manuscripts read “Judea,” and several modern translations follow them. Did Luke send Jesus south while Mark keeps Him in Galilee?

points.label: Luke’s wide use of “Judea”
points.text: Luke sometimes uses Judea for the whole land of the Jews, Galilee included. Herod the Great is called “the king of Judea” (Luke 1:5), though he ruled Galilee too. After a miracle at Nain in Galilee, the report went “throughout all Judea” (Luke 7:17). Jesus’ accusers say He taught “throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee” (Luke 23:5).

points.label: The setting is Galilee
points.text: Luke has just placed Jesus in Capernaum, “a city of Galilee” (Luke 4:31), and next finds Him by the Lake of Gennesaret (Luke 5:1). With either reading, the tour fits the Galilean towns Mark describes.

fit.note: Whichever reading Luke wrote, his wider use of “Judea” agrees with Mark. No error is required.
fit.short: Some manuscripts read “Judea” in Luke 4:44. Luke often uses Judea for the whole Jewish land, Galilee included.

scene.label: A solitary place
scene.text: Galilee’s people lived close together in towns and villages, so solitude meant going out past the houses into the hills or along the empty shore. Mark’s word for the place is the one he used for the wilderness where Jesus was tempted (Mark 1:12–13).

scene.label: The next towns
scene.text: Josephus, who later commanded Jewish forces in Galilee, counted more than two hundred cities and villages in the region. Many lay within a morning’s walk of one another, and most towns of any size had a synagogue where Jesus could find a congregation on the Sabbath.

scene.label: All Syria
scene.text: Syria was the large Roman province to the north and northeast, governed from Antioch. Trade roads between the coast, Damascus and the east ran through Galilee, and news of Jesus traveled with them into Gentile country.

scene.label: Decapolis and beyond the Jordan
scene.text: Decapolis is Greek for ten cities: a league of Greek-speaking towns, most of them east of the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan, with pagan temples and Gentile ways. “Beyond the Jordan” is Perea, on the east bank. Matthew’s list reaches from Jerusalem to Galilee and across the Jordan; Samaria, which lay between Judea and Galilee, is not named.

scene.label: Epileptics
scene.text: Matthew lists the demon-possessed separately from epileptics and paralytics. The Gospels do not treat every illness as the work of demons, though in one case seizures were (Matthew 17:15–18).

witnesses.matthew: Gives no morning scene. He sums up Jesus’ Galilean work as teaching, preaching and healing, and repeats that summary almost word for word in 9:35. Between the two stand the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7) and the miracles of chapters 8–9: the King’s words, then the King’s works.
witnesses.mark: Tells it as an eyewitness, likely Peter, remembered it: the hour before light, Simon leading the search, the blunt “Everyone is looking for You.” Mark’s word for “searched” is a strong one, used of hunting someone down. In Mark, Jesus goes off to pray three times, each by night: here, after feeding the five thousand (6:46), and in Gethsemane (14:32–39).
witnesses.luke: Notes Jesus’ prayers more often than the others, yet does not mention prayer here. He keeps the focus on the crowd that tried to hold Jesus and on His answer, “I must preach the kingdom of God to the other cities also.” That small word “must” runs through Luke for the path the Father set (2:49; 9:22; 24:7).

seeing.reveals: Jesus knew why He had come, and a grateful town could not change it. The Son who met His Father alone before dawn would not be kept by Capernaum; He was sent to preach to all.
seeing.living: Success can pull as hard as failure. Capernaum wanted to keep Jesus, and His friends thought the crowd was the point. Before you let the loudest demand set your course, take it to the Father, as Jesus did, and ask what He has sent you to do.
seeing.ponder: Who is setting the direction of your days: the people looking for you, or the Father who sent you?

preaching.big_idea: In prayer before dawn, Jesus held to His purpose when success begged Him to stay.
outline: Alone with the Father before dawn (35)
preaching.watch_for: Jesus’ words “for this purpose I have come forth” (38) might mean simply that He had left Capernaum. Luke’s parallel, “for this purpose I have been sent” (Luke 4:43), shows the deeper sense: the Father sent Him to preach.
